This page attempts to provide a complete overview over the scientific processes represented by QUINCY. 

As any model documentation, it will lag behind the actual implementation in the code, and interested users
are advised to consult the inline documentation for potential updates. @sec-structure
summarises the general structure and vertical discretisation of vegetation and soil. @sec-assimi
describes the canopy processes, such as photosynthesis and stomatal coupling. @sec-veg introduces
vegetation growth, turnover and dynamics. Soil biogeochemistry is described in
@sec-soil-biogeochemistry. @sec-rad describes the simplified QUINCY radiation scheme, surface energy
balance and soil hydrology.

# General model structure and discretisation {#sec-structure}

Each gridcell of the models is subdivided into nested tiles, each of which is occupied by one
specific vegetation-type, representing a plant functional type (PFT, see Sect. @sec-pfts-cfts), or can be bare soil, permitting energy, water and soil biogeochemistry processes to occur in the absence of living vegetation. The number of tiles per
gridcell is flexible, making it is easy to implement more/different PFTs in the future. 

Vegetation is represented by an average individual composed of a range of structural pools
(leaves, sapwood, heartwood, coarse roots, fine roots, and fruit), a fast overturning, respiring
non-structural pool (labile), as well as a seasonal, non-respiring, and non-structural storage pool
(reserve). Tree vegetation types are furthermore characterised by their height (m), diameter (m),
and stand density ($\mathrm{m^{-2}}$). Soil biogeochemistry is represented using five organic pools:
metabolic (met), structural (str) and and woody (wl) litter, as well as fast (f) and slow (s)
overturning soil organic matter. Each of these pools contains carbon (C), nitrogen (N) and
phosphorus (P), as well as $\mathrm{^{13}C}$, $\mathrm{^{14}C}$, and $\mathrm{^{15}N}$. The unit of
the pools is $\mathrm{mol \ X \ m^{-2}}$ for vegetation and $\mathrm{mol \ X \ m^{-3}}$ for soil
biogeochemical pools, where $X$ represents any of these elements. In addition, the model represents
the following soil biogeochemical pools ($\mathrm{NH_4}$, $\mathrm{NO_3}$, $\mathrm{NO_y}$,
$\mathrm{N_2O}$, $\mathrm{N_2}$, and $\mathrm{PO_4}$), with equivalent units.

The model operates on a half-hourly time-scale (denoted as $dt$), when run offline, or at the step of the atmospheric model when run coupled. Some vegetation and soil biogeochemical processes are assumed
to respond to these instantaneous conditions and associated fluxes with a process-specific lag time
($\tau_{mavg}^{process}$, see @tbl-processes:mavg_period), representing a form of memory for
instance in the calculation of allocation or vegetation dynamic responses. Where appropriate, the
fluxes or pool sizes are calculated as running means with a time-averaging filter as

$$
\begin{align}
X_{mavg,new}^{process} &= X_{mavg,old}^{process} \times (1 - \omega) + X_{current} \times \omega, where\\
&\omega = \frac{dt}{\tau_{mavg}^{process}}
\end{align}
$$

where $X_{current}$ is the instantaneous state or flux of interest, and $X_{mavg,old}^{process}$, as
well as $X_{mavg,new}^{process}$ are the averaged values of the previous and current time step,
respectively.

## Plant and crop functional types {#sec-pfts-cfts}

QUINCY distinguishes twelve plant functional types (PFTs) that each can occupy one of the tiles of a grid cell. Of these, there are eight natural PFTs (moist and dry evergreen broadleaved trees, moist and cold deciduous broadleaved trees, evergreen and deciduous coniferous trees, C3 and C4 herbaceous vegetation, see @Thum:2019mm), as well as four anthropogenic PFTs (C3 and C4 pasture, as well as C3 and C4 crops). 

While pasture PFTs are simply herbacous PFTs exposed to higher grazing pressures and fertilisation, croplands in QUINCY are represented following the approach of AgroIBIS (@kucharik:2000gbc, @kucharik:2003jeq), as implemented in CLM5 (@Levis:2018cc, @clm5:2025git). As CLM5, QUINCY includes five actively managed C3 crop types (wheat, cotton, rice, temperate soybean, tropical soybean) and three actively managed C4 crop types (temperate corn, tropical corn, and sugarcane). As all ICON-Land tiles, crop tiles have their own vegetation and soil biogeochemical pools and are unaffected by processes (including disturbance) of neighbouring tiles. However, currently crop tiles still share soil moisture dynamics with natural tiles. As a result, ICON-Land currently does not include a representation of cropland irrigation. 

## Vertical discretisation {#sec-vertical-discretisation}

The canopy is discretised into 10 layers (denoted by subscript $cl$), with exponentially increasing
layer depth ($LAI_{cl}$) to allow for a better resolution of canopy processes in areas of high light
and nitrogen gradients. Total foliage N ($N_{leaf}$) is distributed to each canopy layer $cl$,
following

$$
\label{eq-veg:canopy_n_distribution}
\begin{align}
N_{leaf,cl} &= N_{leaf,cl=1} \times e^{-k_n \times LAI_c}, where \\
&N_{leaf,cl=1} = \frac{k_n}{1-e^{-k_n \times LAI}} N_{leaf}  
\end{align}
$$

where $LAI_c$ is the cumulative leaf area above the centre-point of the canopy layer, and $LAI$ the
total leaf area, such that less N is allocated to the lower, darker canopy layers, in accordance
with observations of canopy N distribution [@Niinemets:1998].

All soil state-variables (temperature, moisture, texture, soil biogeochemical pools) and fluxes are
discretised into distinct soil layers (denoted by subscript $sl$), with a flexible number of layers depending on model configuration (typically either 5 for global applications and 15 for site-level applications). Layer thickness increases exponentially
with increasing layer depth up to a total depth of 9.5 m, and with a minimum layer thickness for the
top layer of 0.065 m. Fine roots and coarse roots are assumed to be distributed in exponentially
decreasing density along the soil profile according to

$$
\label{eq:veg-root-distribution}
\begin{align}
X_{root,sl} &= X_{root,sl=1} \times e^{-k_{rd} \times depth_{sl}}, where \\
&X_{root,sl=1} = \frac{k_{rd}}{1-e^{-k_{rd} \times depth_r}} X_{root}
\end{align}
$$

where $k_{rd}$ is a PFT-specific parameter (see [Table 6.12](#tbl-lctlib:description),
@Jackson:1996tr), $depth_{sl}$ the depth of the soil layer's mid point, $depth_r$ the rooting depth,
derived from site characteristics and $X_{root}$ the respective fine or coarse root mass. Root growth is inhibited in frozen soil layers. 

For clarity in the following, the subscript for canopy and soil layer is ignored if processes are
treated similarly across layers.

# Canopy processes {#sec-assimi}

## Canopy nitrogen allocation {#sec-veg-foliar-N-fractions}

The leaf area index ($LAI$) and canopy nitrogen content ($N_{leaf}$) are dynamic properties of the
model, as described in Section , and are discretised to canopy layers given by
$\Eqref{eq:veg-root-distribution}$. $N_{leaf,cl}$ is partitioned into photosynthetic and
non-photosynthetic, or structural, N. The fraction of structural N ($fN_{struc,cl}$) is calculated
as a function of the total leaf N in the respective canopy layer:

$$
\label{eq-veg:struc_n}
fN_{struc,cl}=k^{struc}_0-k^{struc}_1 N_{leaf,cl}
$$

where $k^{struc}_0$ and $k^{struc}_1$ are empirical parameters.

The photosynthetic N is further separated into the fraction that is associated with Rubisco
($fN_{rub}$), electron transport ($fN_{et}$), chlorophyll ($fN_{chl}$) and, in the case of C4 plants, PEP carboxylase ($fN_{pepc}$).

The fraction of N in chlorophyll for each layer is calculated as decreasing with canopy depth:

$$
\label{eq-canopy_chl}
fN_{chl}=\frac{k_0^{chl} - k_1^{chl} e^{-k_{fn}^{chl} LAI_c}} {a_{chl}^n},
$$

where $k_0^{chl}$, $k_1^{chl}$ and $k^{chl}$ are empirical parameters, $a_{chl}^n$ is the molecular
N content of chlorophyll.

The values of $fN_{rub}$ and $fN_{et}$ are calculated assuming a fixed ratio of the $V_{cmax}$ and
$J_{max}$ photosynthetic parameters at 25°C, $r_{J2V}$, given the calculated values of the
structural and photosynthetic fractions. The PEP carboxylase fraction, $fN_{pep}$, is considered to be a constant.

## Leaf-level net photosynthesis {#sec-assimi-leaf-ps}

The calculation of leaf-level photosynthesis is based on @Kull:1998cr, extended for C4
photosynthesis according to @Friend:2009tf, and with the temperature response curves as described
in @Bernacchi:2001wv. Unless stated otherwise, temperature sensitivities follow the form:

$$
\label{eq-ps_t_sensitivity}
f_x(T_{air}) = e^{E_0^x - E_1^x/(R\times T_{air})}
$$

where $T_{air}$ is the air temperature ($\mathrm{K}$), $R$ is the universal gas constant
($\mathrm{J mol^{-1} K^{-1}}$), and the process-wise $E_0^x$ and $E_1^x$ are given in
@tbl-assimi:param.

Photosynthesis and stomatal conductance are calculated for the mid-points of each canopy layer and
light-quality class (sunlit and shaded; as defined in Sect. @sec-vertical-discretisation). For clarity, the subscript $_{cl}$ is
omitted in this section.

In light-saturated conditions, gross photosynthesis ($A_g$) in C3 plants is calculated as the
minimum of two potential rates, The electron-transport capacity limited carboxylation ($A_j$) and
the Rubisco-limited rate of photosynthesis ($A_v$). $A_j$ is given by

$$
\label{eq:jmax}
\begin{align}
A_j=& m_1 \times J_{max}, where \\
&m_1=\frac{c_i}{c_i+2\times \Gamma^{*}}, \\
&J_{max} = n_1 \times N_{leaf},  \\
&n_1 = g_{jmax}(T) \times \beta_{soil}^{ps} \times \beta_{sinklim}^{ps} \times  \beta_{soa}^{ps} \times j_{max}^n \times fN_{et}
\end{align}
$$

where $c_i$ is the intercellular partial pressure of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ ($\mathrm{Pa}$, [Eq.
2.18](#eq-stomatal_coupling)), and $\Gamma^{*}$ is the $\mathrm{CO_2}$ compensation point in the
absence of dark respiration. $\beta_{sinklim}^{ps}$ is a signal to reduce photosynthesis in the case
of sink limitation ([Eq. 3.24](#eq-sinklim_c)) and $\beta_{soa}^{ps}$ is accounting for the effect
of low-temperature acclimation in the evergreen species ($\Eqref{eq:veg-soa}$). 

Excessive soil moisture constraints (as discussed in @Rogers:2017np) are assumed to reduce light-saturated
photosynthetic activity by:

$$
\beta_{soil}^{ps} = \sum_{i=1}^{nsoil} \times fract_{root,i} \times (1 - \frac{\Psi_{soil,i}}{\Psi_{leaf}^{min}}),
$$

where $fract_{root,i}$ is the fraction of fine roots in the $i^{th}$ soil layer, $\Psi_{soil,i}$ is the soil water potential in the $i^{th}$ soil layer, ([Eq.6.19](#eq-sse:soil_matrix_potential)), and $\Psi_{leaf}^{min}$ is the PFT-specific minimum leaf water
potential. 

The temperature sensitivity of electron transport is assumed to follow the bell-shaped
form described by @June:2004kj, where $T_{jmax}^{opt}$ is the optimum temperature for $J_{max}$
according to @Friend:2010je, as follows:

$$
\label{eq:tjmax}
\begin{align}
g_{jmax}(T_{air}) =& e^{-\left({\frac{T_{air}-\bar{T}_{jmax}^{opt}}{T_{\Omega}}}\right)^2},\\
&T_{jmax}^{opt} = k0_{jmax}^{topt} + k1_{jmax}^{topt} \times T_{air}; T_{jmax,min}^{opt} < T_{jmax}^{opt} \le T_{jmax,max}^{opt},
\end{align}
$$

where $T_{\Omega}$ is a PFT-specific parameter, $k0_{jmax}^{topt}$ and $k1_{jmax}^{topt}$ are
parameters, $T_{air}$ is the air temperature, and $\bar{T}_{jmax}^{opt}$ in $\Eqref{eq:tjmax}$ is
the mean of the daytime $T_{jmax}^{opt}$ over the past few days ($\tau_{mavg}^{jmax}$), thereby
accounting for temperature acclimation of photosynthesis as in [@Friend:2010je].

$A_v$ is given by

$$
\label{eq-vcmax}
\begin{align}
A_v=&  m_2 \times V_{cmax}, where \\
&m_2 = \frac{c_i}{c_i + k_c (1+O_i/k_o)},\\
&V_{cmax} = n_2 \times N_{leaf} \\
&n_2 =  f_{vcmax}(T) \times \beta_{soil}^{ps} \times \beta_{sinklim}^{ps}\times \beta_{soa}^{ps} \times v_{cmax}^n \times fN_{rub}
\end{align}
$$

where $O_i$ is the intercellular partial pressure of $\mathrm{O_2}$, and $k_c$ and $k_o$ are the
Michaelis-Menten constants for $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and $\mathrm{O_2}$ respectively, derived $E^{kc}_0$,
$E^{kc}_1$, or $E^{ko}_0$, $E^{ko}_0$ using [Eq. 2.3](#eq-ps_t_sensitivity).

The N-specific light-saturated rate of C3 photosynthesis can then be calculated as:

$$
m_{sat} = min(n_1 \times m_1, n_2 \times m_2)
$$

@Friend:2009tf adjusted the scheme by @Kull:1998cr using the Collatz formulation of C4
photosynthesis [@Collatz:1992us]. The simplified assumption is that $A_j$ and $A_v$ can be
calculated as above, but at saturating $c_i$ ($c_{i,max}$). Bundle-sheath transport limitation
($A_p$) is then further limiting C4 photosynthesis, given by

$$
\label{eq-pepc}
\begin{align}
A_p=& V_{pmax} \times m_3, where \\
&V_{pmax} = n_3 \times N_{leaf} \\
&n_3 =  g_{pepc}(T) \times v_{pepc}^n \times fN_{pepc}, \\
&m_3 = \frac{c_i}{p},
\end{align}
$$

where the temperature response is

$$
\label{eq-pepc-t-sensitivity}
g_{pepc}(T) = 2^{(T - T_{ref}^{pepc})/ T_{base}^{pepc}}
$$

The N-specific light-saturated rate of C4 photosynthesis can be calculated as

$$
m_{sat} = min(n_1 \times m_1, n_2 \times m_2, n_3 \times m_3)
$$

The light-harvesting limited rate of photosynthesis ($A_h$) can be written as

$$
\label{eq:ps-lightharvesting}
\begin{align}
A_h =&  m_1 \times \alpha_i \times PPFD_a,\\
&PPFD_a = PPFD_0 (1-e^{-k_a \times C_{chl}}), where\\
&C_{chl} = a_{chl}^n \times fN_{chl} \times N_{leaf}
\end{align}
$$

where $\alpha_i$ is the intrinsic quantum efficiency for $\mathrm{CO_2}$ uptake, $PPFD_0$ is the
photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD) penetrating sunlit or shaded foliage, converted from the
adsorbed radiation of the canopy layer ([Eq. 6.9](#eq-rad:a_shadesunlit)), and $k_a$ as well as
$a_{chl}^n$ are parameters specified in @tbl-assimi:param.

As @Kull:1998cr show, this system of equations ($\Eqref{eq:jmax}$ -
$\Eqref{eq:ps-lightharvesting}$) can be solved to yield gross photosynthesis ($A _g$) for one canopy
layer and light-class as:

$$
\begin{align}
A _g = (1-\frac{\Gamma^{*}}{c_i}) &[m_{sat}N_{sat}+\alpha_i PPFD_a (e^{-k_a n_3 N_{sat}}-e^{-k_a n_3 N_{leaf}}), where\\
N_{lim} &=  - \frac{ln(m_{sat}/[\alpha_i PPFD k_a n_3 m_1])}{k_a n_3}, and \\
&N_{lim} < 0: N_{sat}=0\\
&N_{lim} < N_{leaf}: N_{sat}=N_{lim}\\
&N_{lim} \ge N_{leaf}: N_{sat}=N_{leaf}
\end{align}
$$

## Thermal acclimation of photosynthesis

For evergreen PFTs, recovery of photosynthesis in spring is delayed according to the state
of acclimation ($S$) to air temperature, which reduces photosynthesis in spring until acclimation is
reached [@Makela:2004]. $S$ is calculated as

$$
\label{eq:veg-soa}
\frac{dS}{dt} = \frac{1}{\tau_{soa}}(T_{air}-S)
$$

where $\tau_{soa}$ is a time constant. The reduction factor for Rubisco- and electron transport
limited photosynthesis ($\beta_{soa}$) is calculated as

$$
\label{eq-veg-beta-soa}
\beta_{soa} = \frac{(S - T_{min}^{soa})}{(T_{max}^{soa}-T_{min}^{soa})}
$$

where $T_{min}^{soa}$ and $T_{max}^{soa}$ are parameters and $\beta_{soa}$ is constrained to the
range 0.1 and 1.

## Photosynthetic sink limitation {#sec-veg-sinklim}

In the case that the labile carbon pool exceeds its target size substantially because growth is
limited by temperature, moisture, or because sufficient nutrients are lacking to allow growth ([Eq.
3.9](#eq-veg:growth_rate_x)), sink-limitation down-regulates photosynthetic activity so that:

$$
\label{eq-sinklim-c}
\begin{align}
    \beta_{sinklim}^{ps} &= \beta_{sinklim,min}^{ps} + (1 - \beta_{sinklim,min}^{ps}) \times e^{-(\lambda_{sinklim}^{ps} \times X)^{k_{sinklim}^{ps}}}, where \\
    &X= \frac{C_{labile} - C_{labile}^{target}}{C_{labile}^{target}}
\end{align}
$$

Here, $\beta_{sinklim, min}$, $\lambda_{sinklim}^{ps}$ and $k_{sinklim}^{ps}$ are parameters (see
[Table 6.4](#tbl-veg:param)) and $C_{labile}^{target}$ is the target value for the labile pool ([Eq.
3.19](#eq-target_labile)).

In addition, if the C:N or N:P ratios of the labile pool exceed those of the target labile pool, the
sink limitation factor is further modified as a function of the stoichiometric ratio of the labile
pool and that of the labile target as:

$$
\label{eq-sinklim-cnp}
\beta_{sinklim}^{ps} = \beta_{sinklim}^{ps} \times min(1,\frac{\chi^{N:C}_{labile}}{k^{CNP}_{sinklim} \times \chi^{N:C}_{labile,target}}, \frac{\chi^{P:N}_{labile}}{k^{CNP}_{sinklim} \times \chi^{P:N}_{labile,target}})
$$

where $k^{CNP}_{sinklim}$ is a parameter.

## Stomatal coupling {#sec-assimi-stomatal-coupling}

The combination of leaf-level net photosynthesis ($A_{n,cl}$), stomatal conductance ($g_{s,cl}$),
and leaf internal $\mathrm{CO_2}$ concentration ($c_{i,cl}$) satisfying
$\Eqref{eq:stomatal-coupling}$ is sought iteratively for each canopy layer:

$$
\label{eq:stomatal-coupling}
\begin{align}
A_n &= (A_{g,sunlit} \times f_{sunlit} + A_{g,shaded} \times (1- f_{sunlit})) - R_l\\
g_s &= max(g_0, D_{turb}^{wv2co2} \times (1 + g_1) \frac{A_n \beta_{air}\beta_{soil}^{gs}}{c_a}) \times R  \times T_{air} / p\\
c_i &= c_1 \times c_a - c_2 \times A_n \times ( \frac{D_{air}^{wv2co2}}{g_s} + \frac{D_{turb}^{wv2co2}}{g_a} ) \times R \times T_{air} 
\end{align}
$$

where $f_{sunlit}$ is the fraction of sunlit leaves in a canopy layer (see [Eq.
6.8](#eq-rad:fsunlit)), $R_l$ is the maintenance respiration of leaves (see Sect. @sec-veg-MaintResp), $g_0$ and $g_1$
are PFT-specific parameters, $R$ is the molar gas constant, $T_{air}$ is air temperature (K), $p$
air pressure (Pa), $c_1$ converts $\mathrm{CO_2}$ concentration from ppm to Pa, $c_2$ converts
$\mathrm{\mu mol m^{-2} s^{-1}}$ to $\mathrm{mol m^{-2} s^{-1}}$, $g_a$ is the aerodynamic
conductance, and the $D$'s are the diffusion coefficient corrections for $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and water [@Bonan:2015].

$\beta_{air}$ is the response of stomata to atmospheric dryness (@Medlyn:2011aa], @Knauer:2015dh)

$$
\beta_{air} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{VPD}},
$$

and $\beta_{soil}^{gs}$ is the stomatal response to soil moisture, described by:

$$
\label{eq-veg-beta-soil-gs}
\beta_{soil}^{gs} = \sum_{i=1}^{nsoil} \times fract_{root,i} \times (1 - \frac{\Psi_{soil,i}}{\Psi_{leaf}^{min}}),
$$

where $fract_{root,i}$ is the fraction of fine roots in the $i^{th}$ soil layer, $\Psi_{soil,i}$ is the soil water potential in the $i^{th}$ soil layer, ([Eq.6.19](#eq-sse:soil_matrix_potential)), and $\Psi_{leaf}^{min}$ is the PFT-specific minimum leaf water potential. 

## Canopy integration {#canopy-integration}

Canopy-level fluxes are derived by summing the product of layer-level fluxes or state-variables and
the depth of the layer

$$
F = \sum_{cl=1}^{ncanopy} F_{cl} \times LAI_{cl},
$$

where $F$ is the canopy-level equivalent of a leaf-level variable $F_{cl}$ (per unit leaf-area),
such as gross photosynthesis ($A_g$), net photosynthesis ($A_n$), and leaf-level stomatal
conductance ($g_s$), (see Sect. @sec-assimi-leaf-ps and @sec-assimi-stomatal-coupling) and $LAI_{cl}$ is the leaf area index of the canopy layer. The
resulting canopy net assimilation $A_g$ is used as input to the vegetation model ([Eq.
3.1](#eq-veg:labile_pool_dynamics)), the canopy conductance ($G_s$) is used for the calculation of
ecosystem transpiration ([Eq. 6.14](#eq-sse_surface_energy_balance)).

# Vegetation growth, turnover and dynamics {#sec-veg}

## Labile pool dynamics {#sec-labile-pool}

The growth of a plant is dependent on the partitioning of its labile resource to new tissue growth,
storage production, as well as -- in the case of C -- respiration for maintenance and resource
uptake:

$$
\label{eq-veg-labile-pool-dynamics}
\begin{align}
\frac{dC_{labile}}{dt} &= A_g + \Delta S_C - R_m - R_r - (1 + f_{resp,growth}) \times G_C \\
\frac{dN_{labile}}{dt} &= U_{root,N} + F_{sBNF} + \Delta S_N  - G_N  \\
\frac{dP_{labile}}{dt} &= U_{root,P} + \Delta S_P - G_P 
\end{align}
$$

where $R_m$ is maintenance respiration, $R_r$ is resource uptake respiration (for both see Sect. @sec-veg-MaintResp),
$\Delta S_X$ is the net exchange between the labile and reserve pool (Sect. @sec-veg-reserve), $f_{resp,growth}$ is
the constant fraction of respiration associated with growth, $G_X$ are the growth rates to build new
tissues, $U_{root,X}$ are nutrient rates of root uptake, and $F_{sBNF}$ is the symbiontic N fixation rate.

## Maintenance respiration {#sec-veg-MaintResp}

Maintenance respiration for every vegetation pool ($i$) is estimated from its N content ($N_i$) as

$$
\label{eq-veg:respiration}
R_{m,i}=f_{temp} \times f_{resp,maint}^{i} \times N_i
$$

where $f_{resp, maint}^{i}$ is the maintenance respiration per unit N, which differs between woody
and non-woody pools, and $f_{temp}$ is the instantaneous temperature response of respiration
[@Lloyd1994-jn]

$$
\label{eq-veg-t-resp}
f_{temp}=e^{t_{k1} (\frac{1}{t_{k2}} - \frac{1} {T - t_{k3}})}
$$

where $t_{k1}, t_{k2}$ and $t_{k3}$ are temperature sensitivity parameters and $T$ is the
instantaneous air or soil temperature for above- and belowground tissues, respectively. Following @Atkin:2014, the basal respiration rate acclimates to temperature

$$
\label{eq-veg-resp-acclim}
f_{maint\_rate}=f_{maint\_rate,ref}10^{f_{resp\_acclim}(T_{acclim}-T_{acclim,ref})}
$$

where $f_{maint\_rate,ref}$ is the N-specific maintenance respiration rate at the temperature
$T_{acclim,ref}$, $f_{resp\_acclim}$ is the slope of the temperature acclimation and $T_{acclim}$ is
the running average of air or soil temperature ($\tau_{mavg}^{resp}$), respectively.

Respiration costs for the transformation of $\mathrm{NH_4}$ or $\mathrm{NO_3}$ into organic nitrogen is given by specific costs ($cost_i$, @Zerihun:1998) and the actual uptake rate ($U_{plant,i}$) as

$$
\label{eq-veg-nutrient-costs}
R_{r,i}=cost_{i} \times U_{plant,i}
$$

where $i$ is either $\mathrm{NH_4}$ or $\mathrm{NO_3}$.

Respiration associated with symbiotic fixation of is given by the specific costs of N fixation ($cost_{bnf,symb}$) and the actual rate of symbiotic N fixation (see Sect. @sec-veg-nfixation).

$$
\label{eq-veg-bnf-costs}
R_{r,bnf}=cost_{bnf} \times F_{sBNF}
$$

## Growth {#sec-growth}

The potential, source-limited growth rate ($G^{*}_X$) is given by the product of the maximum
turnover rate of the labile pool ($1/\tau_{labile}$) and the labile pool size ($X_{labile}$). Three
sink limitation processes operate, which control the down-regulation of this potential growth rate
to the actual growth rates ($G_X$):

-   the temperature and moisture sensitivity of the meristem ([Eq. 3.6](#eq-veg:k0_lab));

-   the requirement for maintenance respiration ([Eq. 3.2](#eq-veg:respiration)), which takes
    priority over new growth; and

-   the co-limitation of growth by the nutrients required to grow specific pools ([Eq.
    3.9](#eq-veg:growth_rate)).

The meteorological/environmental control on the meristem mechanism is represented by a reduction of
the maximum turnover rate at low temperatures and low soil moisture conditions.

$$
\label{eq-veg-k0-lab}
k^{*}_{labile} = \frac{1}{\tau_{labile}} \times e^{-(\lambda^{labile}_{temp}\times T_{air})^{k^{labile}_{temp}}} \times e^{-(\lambda^{labile}_{\Theta}\times \Theta)^{k^{labile}_{\Theta}}}
$$

where $T_{air}$ is air temperature in degrees Celsius, $\Theta$ is the fractional soil moisture
content ([Eq. 6.18](#eq-sse:theta)), and the $\lambda$ and $k$ are parameters. $k^{*}_{labile}$ is
set to zero outside the growing season (see Sect. @sec-veg-phen).

Respiration is assumed to have priority over growth. However, under severe C deficit, the meristem
activity also down-regulates maintenance and resource uptake respiration. To ensure that carbon
growth ($G_C$) does not exceed the size of the labile carbon pool, the turnover rate of the labile
pool to growth is corrected by the current respiration rate, and constrained to positive solutions:

$$
\label{eq-growth-c}
G^{*}_C = k^{*}_{labile} \times C_{labile} \times dt - R_m - R_r; G^{*}_C \ge 0
$$

Given $G^{*}_C$, and the stoichiometric requirements for biomass growth ($req^{growth}_{NC}$, and
$req^{growth}_{PN}$, respectively):

$$
\label{eq-veg-req-growth}
req^{growth}_{XY} = \sum^{pools}_{i}{f^{i}_{alloc} \times \frac{X_i}{Y_i}}
$$

where $f^{i}_{alloc}$ are the allocation fractions (Sect. @sec-veg-allocation) to each pool $i$, and $\frac{X_i}{Y_i}$
are the target stoichiometries of C:N:P (Sect. @sec-veg-stoichem) of the leaf, fine root, coarse root, sapwood, and
fruits pools. The actual growth rates can be calculated as

$$
\label{eq-veg-growth-rate}
\begin{align}
G_P &= req^{growth}_{N:P} \times G_N = req^{growth}_{P:N} \times req^{growth}_{N:C} \times G_C \\
&G_C \le G^{*}_C \\
&G_N \le \frac{k^{nut}_{labile}}{\tau_{labile}} \times N_{labile} \times dt \\
&G_P \le \frac{(k^{nut}_{labile})^2}{\tau_{labile}} \times P_{labile} \times dt,
\end{align}
$$

Note that only the minimum of the three rates in [Eq. 3.9](#eq-veg-growth-rate) can actually be
realised. The other two growth rates are adjusted, implying a relative accumulation of these
elements in the labile pool. The use of $k^{nut}_{labile}$ implies a stronger mobilisation capacity
for nutrients than for carbon growth. The assumption behind this is that the temperature and
moisture control of the meristem is already accounted for by $G_C$, and that the plant is able to
mobilise the required nutrients from the labile pool to support this growth.

Outside the growing season, all growth fluxes are set to zero (see Sect. @sec-veg-phen).

## Partitioning of growth to plant organs {#sec-veg-allocation}

### Natural Plant Functional Types

The labile pool partitioned to growth is first split into reproductive (fruit pool) and structural
(leaves, fine and coarse roots and sap wood) growth. The latter is then further subdivided following
a functional balance relationship between the structural pools [@Zaehle:2010cz].

The fraction of carbon growth allocated to fruit depends on the ability of the plant to build
reserves ($\Delta S_C$, see Sect. @sec-veg-reserve), implying that fruit growth is suppressed during phases of rapid
leaf growth (beginning of the growing season), as well as periods of C starvation (e.g. severe drought).

$$
\label{eq-veg-falloc-fruit}
f^{fruit}_{alloc,C} = k1^{fruit}_{alloc} + (k2^{fruit}_{alloc} - k1^{fruit}_{alloc}) \times exp^{-(\lambda^{fruit}_{alloc}\times (\Delta S_C+k3^{fruit}_{alloc}))^{k4^{fruit}_{alloc}}}
$$

where the maximum fraction of allocation to fruits ($k2^{fruit}_{alloc}$) is a PFT-specific
parameter. The allocation of the remaining growth ($(1-f^{fruit}_{alloc,C}) \times G_C$) to the
structural pools leaves, fine root, coarse roots, and sapwood follows a set of following allometric
relationships [@Zaehle:2010cz].

For both trees and grasses, fine root and leaves are assumed to be in homeostatic balance described
as

$$
\label{eq-veg-ltor}
C_{leaf} =  f^{ltor}_{N|P|H_20} \times k_{rtos} \times \frac{C_{leaf}}{C_{sap\_wood}} \times C_{fine\_root}
$$

where $k_{rtos}$ is a PFT-specific parameter and $f^{ltor}$ is a function describing the response of
the leaf to root ratio to nutrient and water limitation. It is calculated as the minimum of three
functions describing N, P and water limitation respectively, calculated as:

$$
\label{eq-veg-dynamic-alloc}
f^{ltor} = min(\frac{N_{labile}/C_{labile}}{req^{growth}_{NC}},\frac{P_{labile}/N_{labile}}{req^{growth}_{PN}},\frac{W_{soil,root}}{W^{alloc}_{soil,crit}})
$$

$X_{labile}$ refers to the content of the respective element in the labile pool and
$req^{growth}_{NC}$ and $req^{growth}_{PN}$ are the N:C and P:N ratios required for growth,
respectively (see eqn. [Eq. 3.8](#eq-veg-req-growth)). For the water limited allocation,
$W^{alloc}_{soil,crit}$ is the critical level of soil moisture below which root allocation increases
and $W_{soil,root}$ is calculated as the ratio between the current water content in the root zone
and the water content in the root zone at field capacity.

In grasses, halms are assumed to be a proportion of leaf mass, and no height restrictions apply.

$$
\label{eq-l2s-grass}
C_{leaf} = k_{htol} \times C_{sap\_wood}
$$

In trees and shrubs, leaf and woody biomass are linked through the pipe-model hypothesis (requiring
a constant ratio of leaf area, $LA$, to sapwood area, $SA$)

$$
\label{eq-veg-latosa}
C_{leaf} = \frac{k_{latosa} \times C_{sap\_wood}}{sla \times \rho_{wood} \times H} <=> LA = k_{latosa} \times SA,
$$

where $sla$, $k_{latosa}$, and $\rho_{wood}$ are the PFT-specific specific leaf area, leaf to
sapwood area ratio, and wood density, respectively. $H$ is the mean forest canopy height calculated
as:

$$
\label{eq-veg-allometry}
H = k1_{allom} \times D^{k2_{allom}},
$$

where the diameter at breast height ($D$) is determined from woody biomass, assuming that the entire
trunk is a cylinder. As an extension to the pipe-model theory below-ground, coarse root biomass is
assumed to be proportional to sap wood mass:

$$
\label{eq-veg-coarse-root}
C_{coarse\_root} = k_{ctos} \times C_{sap\_wood}
$$

where $k_{ctos}$ is a PFT-specific parameters.

### Crop Functional Types

At planting, the labile pool of the crop is initialised with a given seed mass ($X_{crop,ini}$), which is taken from the seed-bed pool ($X_{seed-bed}$). Matter in the labile pool can either be used to fuel respiration or be allocated to leaf, fine root, stem or grain pools. Allocation does not follow the pipe-model analogy for natural PFTs, but is based on the allocation coefficients approach from Agro-IBIS (@kucharik:2000gbc, @kucharik:2003jeq), which has been adapted to match the formulation of carbon partitioning in QUINCY. 

The partitioning coefficients to leaves, fine root and stem biomass ($f_{leaf}$, $f_{fine_root}$ and $f_{stem}$, respectively) are determined from the difference between the allometric relationships between leaf and fine root mass ($k_{l2r}$) and leaf to stem mass ($k_{l2s}$), and the state of current carbon mass in leaf, fine root and stem \citep[see][for details]{thum:2019gmd}. These partitioning coefficients are then rescaled to take account of the partitioning coefficient to grains ($f_{grain}$), which is determined independently, such that the mass-balancing equation is satisfied:

$$
1 = f_{leaf} +f_{fine_root} + f_{stem} + f_{grain}
$$

The leaf to fine root allometric ratio ($k_{l2r}$) varies with accumulated heat sum:

$$
\begin{align}
k_{l2r} = 
& l2r_{fin} + (l2r_{init} - l2r_{fin}) \times \notag \\
& \frac{e^{-k_{GDD,grain}}-e^{k_{GDD,grain}*f_{GDD}}}{e^{-k_{GDD,grain}}-1} \notag
\end{align}
$$

where $l2r_{init}$ and $l2r_{fin}$ are the leaf to root mass ratio at emergence and grainfilling, respectively, and $k_{GDD,grain}$ is an empirical parameter. $k_{l2r}$ is constrained a minimum value ($l2r_{min}$) once the LAI of the crop exceeds the CFT-specific $LAI_{max}^{crop}$, effectively reducing carbon allocation to leaves to zero. $f_{GDD}$ a heat sum index, defined as

$$
f({GDD}) = min(\frac{GDD_{cs}}{GDD_{thres}^{grainfilling}} , 1)   
$$

The leaf to stem allometric ratio ($k_{l2s}$) increases with progressing crop maturity as follows

$$
k_{l2s} = \frac{1}{s2l_{init} + s2l_{fin} \times \frac{e^{-k_{GDD}}-e^{k_{GDD}*f({GDD_{cs})}}}{e^{-k_{GDD}}-1}}
$$

where $k_{l2s}$ is the leaf to stem mass ratio and $s2l_{init}$ as well as $s2l_{fin}$ are CFT-specific initial and final stem to leaf mass ratios. 

In the grain-filling period, the fraction of carbon allocation to growth used for grain increases from zero to a CFT-specific maximum partitioning fraction to grain ($f_{grain,max}$) according to 

$$
f_{grain} = f_{grain,max} \times (1 - ( 1- (\frac{GDD_{cs} - GDD_{thres}^{grainfilling}}{GDD_{thres}^{maturity}-GDD_{thres}^{grainfilling}})^{k_{GDD,grain}}) 
$$

Partitioning of nutrients in the labile pool to growth of leaf, fine root, stem and grain follows the same parameterisation as for natural PFTs.

## Tissue stoichiometry {#sec-veg-stoichem}

Following [@Meyerholt:2015hh], C:N:P stoichiometry for slow-overturning structural tissues (sap
wood, coarse roots) as well as fruits, is assumed to be time-invariant and modelled as dependent on
the PFT-specific mean foliar stoichiometry ($\chi^{C:N}_{leaf}$, and $\chi^{N:P}_{leaf}$) and set
ratios (see [Table 6.4](#tbl-veg:param)). Heartwood stoichiometry differs from sapwood stoichiometry
because a fraction of the nutrients are retranslocated ($k^{wood}_{resorb}$) to the labile pool upon
heartwood formation.

Following [@Zaehle:2010cz], the C:N and N:P ratios of leaves are varied in response to the nutrient
demand and supply so that:

$$
\chi^{X:Y}_{leaf|t+1} = \chi^{X:Y}_{leaf} \times (1 + \delta^{\chi}_{leaf} \times \Gamma_{XY} )
$$

where $\chi^{X:Y}_{leaf}$ denotes either the C:N or N:P ratio of the leaves, $\delta^{\chi}_{leaf}$
is a parameter denoting the maximum amount that leaf nutrients can change per timestep and
$\Gamma_{X:Y}$ heuristically accounts for limits to the plasticity of foliar stoichiometry as:

$$
\label{eq-veg-stoichem-dynamic}
    \Gamma_{X:Y} = 
    \left\{
    \begin{array}{ll}
        e^{-(\lambda^{\chi}_{leaf}\frac{ \chi^{X:Y}_{leaf}}{\chi^{X:Y}_{leaf,min}+\chi^{X:Y}_{leaf,max}})^{k^{\chi}_{leaf}}}  & 
        \mbox{if } \chi^{Y:X}_{labile} \leq req^{growth}_{Y:X} \\
        -(1 - e^{-(\lambda^{\chi}_{leaf}\frac{ \chi^{X:Y}_{leaf}}{\chi^{X:Y}_{leaf,min}+\chi^{X:Y}_{leaf,max}})^{k^{\chi}_{leaf}}}) & \mbox{if } \chi^{Y:X}_{labile} > req^{growth}_{Y:X}
    \end{array}
\right.
$$

In the above, $\chi^{X:Y}_{leaf,min}$ and $\chi^{X:Y}_{leaf,max}$ are PFT-specific parameters. The
condition refers to the relationship between the nutrients available for growth in the labile pool
and the nutrients required for growth ([Eq. 3.8](#eq-veg-r0-growth)), averaged at the time-scale of
$\tau_{mavg}^{\chi}$. The stoichiometric ratios of the fine roots vary proportionally to those of
the leaves, whereas the stoichiometry of wood is assumed time-invariant [@Meyerholt:2015hh]. The
stoichiometry of the labile and reserve pools are prognostic properties, as described in Sect. @sec-veg-stoichem.

## Non-structural reserve pool dynamics {#sec-veg-reserve}

The target leaf carbon pool ($C^{target}_{leaf}$) is determined by the current allometry, and
corresponds to the leaf area index implied by current sapwood area.

The target labile carbon pool size buffers short term fluctuations in GPP, and is assumed to
correspond to the maximum of the cumulated $GPP$ or $R_m$ over the turnover time of the labile pool,
while the target of the labile nitrogen and phosphorus pool corresponds to the average
stoichiometric growth requirement over the turnover time of the labile pool:

$$
\label{eq-target-labile}
\begin{align}
C^{target}_{labile} &= max(\int_{t=-{\tau^{0}_{labile}}}^{t=0} GPP \times dt, \int_{t=-{\tau^{0}_{labile}}}^{t=0} R_m\times dt) \\
N^{target}_{labile} &= req^{growth}_{NC} \times C^{target}_{labile}  \\
P^{target}_{labile} &= req^{growth}_{PN} \times N^{target}_{labile} 
\end{align}
$$

The target size of the reserve pool depends on the C required to replace the annual growth of leaves
and fine roots. It is scaled by a PFT-specific constant as a measure of risk avoidance
($k^{target}_{reserve}$), with larger values indicating a preference for storage over growth.

$$
\label{eq-target-storage}
\begin{align}
C^{target}_{reserve} &= min(k_{reserve} \times (1+f_{resp,growth}) \times \frac{LAI^{target}}{sla}, \sum_{i=l,f,s} f_{reserve,max,i} \times C_{i}), where \\
&k_{store} = k^{target}_{reserve} \times ( min(1,\frac{1}{\tau_{leaf}}) + \frac{1}{\tau_{fine\_root} \times R_{leaf:fine\_root}} ) 
\end{align}
$$

where $sla$ the PFT-specific specific leaf area, $\tau_{leaf}$ and
$\tau_{fine\_root}$ are the PFT-specific turnover times of foliage and fine roots, and $R_{leaf:fine\_root}$ is the leaf to root ratio ([Eq. 3.12](#eq-veg:dynamic_alloc)) averaged over the lifetime of the fine roots ($\tau_{mavg}^{root}$). 
$LAI^{target}$ is the target leaf area index, which is calculated differently for tree and herbaceous PFTs. For tree PFTs, $LAI^{target}$ is a function of the implied leaf area calculated from the actual sapwood area (see Sect. @sec-veg-allocation). For herbaceous PFTs, $LAI^{target}$ corresponds to the long-term average LAI. For both PFT types, $LAI^{target}$ is constrained to values between $LAI_{min}$ and $LAI^{target}_{max}$.
The target reserve pool size is limited to a maximum storage capacity of leaves, fine roots and stems, with an assumed maximum fractional storage capacity for each tissue type ($f_{store,i}^{max}$). The N and P target pools are defined in an
equivalent manner, respecting the current target stoichiometry of leaves and fine roots (Sect. @sec-veg-stoichem). 

The net exchange between the labile and reserve pool is calculated as

$$
\label{eq-veg-phimaint}
\begin{align}
\Delta S_X &= \frac{1}{\tau_{labile}} \times (\Phi^{X}_{maint} \times X_{reserve} - \Phi^{X}_{store} \times X_{labile}) \times dt; with \\
&\Phi^{X}_{maint} = e^{-(\lambda^{\Phi}_{maint} \times \frac{X_{labile}}{X^{target}_{labile}})^{k^{\Phi}_{maint}}}, and \\
&\Phi^{X}_{store} = 1 - e^{-(\lambda^{\Phi}_{store} \times \frac{X_{reserve}}{X^{target}_{reserve}})^{k^{\Phi}_{store}}}
\end{align}
$$

where $\lambda^{\Phi}_{maint}$, $k^{\Phi}_{maint}$, $\lambda^{\Phi}_{store}$, and $k^{\Phi}_{store}$
are parameters of a Weibull-type function. Under conditions of severe resource stress (i.e. low
labile pool size corresponding to its target size), the build up of reserves, is reduced according
to

$$
\label{eq-veg-phi-interact}
  \Phi^{X}_{store} = \frac{ 1 - \Phi^{X}_{maint}}{1 - k_{\Phi,inter}} \Phi^{X}_{store},\ if\ \Phi^{X}_{maint} > k_{\Phi,inter}
$$

where $k_{\Phi,inter}$ is a parameter. To support leaf and fine-root growth at the beginning of the
growing season, $\Delta S_X$ is further modified by the phenological pull ($\Phi^{X}_{phen}$) during
the growing season as follows:

$$
\label{eq-veg-phiphen}
\begin{align}
\Delta S_X  &= \Delta S_X + k^{*}_{labile} \times \Phi^{X}_{phen} \times X_{reserve} \times dt, with \\
&\Phi^{X}_{phen} = e^{-(\lambda^{\Phi}_{phen} \times \frac{X_{leaf}}{X^{target}_{leaf}})^{k^{\Phi}_{phen}}} 
\end{align}
$$

where $\lambda^{\Phi}_{phen}$, and $k^{\Phi}_{phen}$ are parameters of a Weibull-type function.


## Phenology {#sec-veg-phen}

### Natural Plant Functional Types

The model differentiates evergreen, cold deciduous, rain deciduous tree and shrub phenological strategies, as well as herbaceous perennial phenological strategies. The start and end of the the growing season are determined by
meteorological triggers and soil moisture. The meteorological variables determining these phenological
triggers are averaged over $\tau_{mavg}^{phen}$, to smooth out the effect of day-to-day climate variability. 

The growing season start for cold deciduous and herbaceous PFTs is described as a function of the accumulated growing degree days ($GDD_{acc}$) as:

$$
\label{eq-phen-gdd}
\begin{align}
 GDD_{acc} &> GDD_{req}^{max} \times exp^{- k^{GDD}_{dormance}\times NDD}, where \\
 &\frac{GDD_{acc}}{dt} = GDD_{acc} + MAX(t_{air} - t_{tair}^{GDD},0.0)
\end{align}
$$

where $GDD_{acc}$ denotes the current growing degree days above the temperature threshold
($t_{air}^{GDD}$), $NDD$ is the number of dormancy days, taken as days since the last growing
season, and $k^{GDD}_{dormance}$ is a PFT-specific parameter relating dormancy to the PFT-specific
maximum growing degree days requirement ($GDD_{req}^{max}$) to account for the chilling requirements
of the buds [@Krinner:2005wg].

For rain deciduous phenology, the start of the growing season is triggered when the soil moisture
stress factor ($\beta_{soil}^{gs}$, see [Eq. 2.19](#eq-veg:beta_soil_gs)) is larger than a
PFT-specific threshold ($\beta_{soil}^{flush}$). This criterion is also applied for herbaceous PFTs
in addition to the $GDD$-criterion.

The end of the growing season for cold deciduous and herbaceous PFTs is triggered by decreasing
average air temperatures below a PFT-specific temperature threshold ($t_{air}^{sen}$). For raingreen
and herbaceous PFTs the end of the growing season is triggered when the soil moisture stress factor
($\beta_{soil}^{gs}$) becomes lower than a PFT-specific threshold ($\beta_{soil}^{sen}$). In
addition, herbaceous PFTs end their growing season, once the weekly carbon balance ($GPP - R_m$)
becomes negative. Senescence is generally only introduced once the leaf age has become larger than a
PFT-specific threshold ($age^{leaf}_{min}$).

The phenology of vegetation, describing the seasonal development of foliage biomass, is then simulated
prognostically given the ability of the plant to grow new tissues, which depends on the size and
turnover of the meristems ([Eq. 3.9](#eq-veg:growth_rate)), as well as the fractional allocation of
growth to plant organs (see Sect. @sec-veg-allocation). Plant growth set to zero outside the growing season
([Eq. 3.9](#eq-veg:growth_rate)). 

While the beginning and ending mark the start and end of tissue production, only the turnover of the leaves is directly affected by phenological triggers. The turnover of all other
tissues is assumed to be constant (see Sect. @sec-veg-turnover). A notable exception are herbaceaous PFTs, in which the growing season ends due to water stress. In these, root shedding occurs at the same rate as leaf shedding.

### Crop Functional Types

Crop growth is divided into four distinct growth stages, (1) planting, (2) emergence, (3) grain filling, (4) harvesting, followed by a CFT-specific fallow period.   

Planting occurs when CFT-specific thresholds for growing degree days ($T_{thres,gdd}^{planting}$), weekly air temperature ($T_{thres,air}^{planting}$), soil temperature ($T_{thres,soil}^{planting}$), soil moisture ($\beta_{thres,soil}^{planting}$) and daylength ($DL_{thres}^{planting}$) are exceeded, and a CFT-specific minimum fallow time ($fdays_{thres}^{planting}$) between crop seasons is passed. Development during the crops season progresses along an index of heat sum ($gdd_{cs}$), defined as 

$$
GDD_{cs} = \sum{(T_{air} - T_{thres,air}^{growth}) \times dt} 
$$

where $T_{air}$ is the ambient air temperature, $T_{thres,air}^{growth}$ a CFT-specific threshold and $dt$ the length of the model time-step. $GDD_{cs} $ is set to zero at the beginning of a new crop season.

Planting immediately starts the next growth phase (emergence), because different to AgroIBIS (@kucharik:2000gbc,@kucharik:2003jeq), the crop mass initialisation occurs to the labile pool instead of the leaf pool, with automatically causes a delay in the emergence of leaves. Emergence lasts until the heat-sum index exceeds a CFT-specific threshold ($GDD_{thres}^{grainfilling}$), or the CFT has reached a CFT-specific maximum LAI ($lai_{max}^{crop}$). One emergence ends, grain filling starts until the heat sum has reached a CFT-specific threshold for maturity ($GDD_{thres}^{maturity}$), or the CFT-specific maximum crop season length ($n_{max}^{season}$) has been reached. In either cases, harvesting is initiated, and the length of the crop season is recorded.

$GDD_{thres}^{maturity}$ depends on local climate, measured as the long-term (20 years) average of crop season GDD  ($\bar{GDD_{cs}}$), as well as a CFT-specific parameter ($fGPP_{mat}$).

$$
GDD_{thres}^{maturity} = fGPP_{mat} \times \bar{GDD_{cs}} 
$$

Solutions of $GDD_{thres}^{maturity}$ are constrained by CFT-specific minimum and maximum GDD requirements ($GDD_{thres,min}^{maturity}$ and $GDD_{thres,max}^{maturity}$, respectively). 

$GDD_{thres}^{grainfilling}$ is a CFT-specific fraction of the GDD requirement for maturity.

$$
GDD_{thres}^{grainfilling} = f_{grainfilling} \times GDD_{thres}^{maturity} 
$$

QUINCY distinguishes temperate crops (wheat, temperate corn, temperate soybean and cotton), for which only one cropping seasons per year is permitted, from tropical crops, which can have multiple cropping seasons per year if potential crop season period permits accumulating at least twice the heat sum requirement for maturity. 

## Tissue turnover and nutrient recycling {#sec-veg-turnover}

The turnover time of most tissue types (fine and coarse roots, sapwood, and fruits) is assumed
constant for each PFT ($\tau_{fine\_root}$, $\tau_{coarse\_root}$, $\tau_{sap\_wood}$, and
$\tau_{fruit}$, respectively). While roots turn directly into litter, only a small
fraction of sapwood ($f_{sap\_wood}^{branch}$) is turned to litter, assuming it is lost as branches
($\tau_{branches}$), whereas the predominant fraction of sapwood turns into non-respiring hardwood
at the timescale of $\tau_{sap\_wood}$. 

In evergreen trees, foliar turnover to litter is assumed to
be constant ($\tau_{leaves}$). For deciduous and herbaceous PFTs only minor turnover happens at
$\tau_{leaves}$ during the growing season. At the end of the growing season (see Sect. @sec-veg-phen), foliar
turnover is set to a constant rate

$$
\label{eq-veg-dec-leaf-turnover}
    f^{leaf}_{turn} = min(f_{shed,max} \times \frac{LAI^{target}}{LAI}, 1)
$$

Resorption of nutrients to the labile pool during litterfall is assumed to only occur during foliage
turnover and heartwood formation at a constant fraction ($k_{resorb}^{X}$), so that:

$$
\label{eq-veg-resorb}
\begin{align}
&flux^{X}_{pool \rightarrow litter} = (1-k_{resorb}^{X}) \times \frac{  X_{pool}}{\tau_{pool}} \times dt, and \\
&flux^{X}_{pool \rightarrow labile} = k_{resorb}^{X} \times \frac{X_{pool}}{\tau_{pool}} \times dt,
\end{align}
$$

where $flux^{X}_{pool \rightarrow litter}$ is the litterfall from any one pool, and
$flux^{X}_{pool \rightarrow labile}$ the retranslocated flux into the labile pool.

Nutrients in living leaf and fine root tissues are constantly recylced between these pools and the labile pool at the time-scale of $\tau_{{nut}\_{recycle}}$.
The freed nutrients enter the labile pool and are replaced by new nutrients of the labile pool
according to the current target C:N:P of the respective pool.

$$
\label{eq-veg-nut-recycling}
\frac{X_{pool}}{dt} = (Y_{pool} \frac{X_{pool}^{target}}{Y_{pool}^{target}} - X_{pool}) \times 1/\tau_{{nut}\_{recycle}},
$$

where $X$ is either N or P, and $Y$ C or N, respectively. The flux from the labile pool is limited
by the turnover rate and size of the labile pool to ascertain that the latter cannot be exhausted.

Turnover of fruits replenishes the seed-bed pool, which - for natural PFTs - turns into litter according to a dedicated turnover time ($\tau_{seed\_bed}$), but which is also used to fuel establishement of new individuals (see Sect. @sec-veg-dynamics). 

For crop functional types, grain turnover is simulated to replenish the seed-bed pool used for initialisation of the crop labile pool in the next crop season (see @sec-veg-allocation). The seed-bed pool is assumed to be protected from turnover, until it reaches $f_{store,max}$ times the requirement for crop initialisation. Once the pool exceeds this amount, the seed-bed turns over to litter, as for natural PFTs.  

## Symbiotic nitrogen fixation {#sec-veg-nfixation}

Symbiotic N fixation follows the approach of @Rastetter:2001aa, as presented by @Meyerholt:2016, but adjusted to the model structure of QUINCY, and with the acclimating temperature response function derived by @Bytnerowicz:2022aa.

$$
\label{eq-veg-n-fixation}
\begin{align}
F_{sBNF} = & v_{max,sbnf} \times f(T_{air}) \times \notag\\
& \frac{cost^{uptake} - cost^{sbnf}}{km_{sbnf}+ cost^{uptake} - cost^{sbnf}} \times C_{fine\_root} 
\end{align} 
$$

where $cost^{sbnf}$ is the carbon cost of N fixation [@Kern:2020tu], $cost^{uptake}$ is the weekly average marginal carbon investment cost per actual fine root N uptake calculated from QUINCY and constrained to values equal or larger than $cost^{sbnf}$, $km_{sbnf}$ an empirical smoothing parameter [@Rastetter:2001aa], and $v_{max,sbnf}$ is a PFT-specific parameter calibrated to match the data presented by @Davies-barnard:2020gb. The temperature sensitivity function $f(T_{air})$ has been re-parameterised as peaked-Arrhenius function with temperature-sensitive activation energy $E_{ed,sbnf}$ and optimum temperature ($T_{opt,sbnf}$, but constant de-activation energy ($E_{ed,sbnf}$) to allow for the acclimation of N fixation with temperature as observed by @Bytnerowicz:2022aa.

## Vegetation dynamics {#sec-veg-dynamics}

To assess stand density, we define for tree functional types the crown area as:

$$
\label{eq-veg-crownarea}
CA = k_{CA} \times D^{k_{rp}}
$$

where $k_{CA}$ and $k_{rp}$ are parameters, $D$ is the tree diameter at breast hight and $CA$ is
constrained to be less then a maximum crown area ($CA_{max}$). Using stand-scale LAI, individuum
density and crown area, the LAI of an individual tree is defined ($LAI_{ind}$), which is used to
calculated the foliage projective cover ($FPC$) as:

$$
\label{eq-veg-fpc}
FPC = CA \times dens_{ind} ( 1 - e^{-k_{fpc} \times LAI_{ind}})
$$

where $k_{fpc}$ is a paramter. To avoid strong seasonal cycles in foliage projective cover for the
calculation of vegetation dynamics [@Krinner:2005wg; @Zaehle:2010cz], $LAI_{ind}$ is diagnosed from
the sapwood area implied by the pipe-model ([Eq. 3.14](#eq-veg:latosa)), implying that $FPC$ is
essentially representing last year's maximum LAI. For grasses, the calculation of $FPC$ is not
required and it is set to zero.

The establishment flux for a PFT is dependent on the size of the seed-bed pool and the average,
PFT-specific seed-bed turnover time ($\tau_{seed,est}$):

$$
\label{eq-veg-flux_est}
flux_{est,X} = f_{dens} \times f_{temp} \times f_{moist} \times \frac{X_{seed\_bed}}{\tau_{seed,est}}
$$

where $f_{temp}$ and $f_{moist}$ represent limitations for establishment at low temperature and low
moisture availability in the form of Weibull-functions with parameters $\lambda_{est}^{env}$ and
$k_{est}^{env}$, where $env$ refers to either weekly air temperature ($T_{air}$) or weekly top-soil
moisture ($\Theta_1$). Density dependency of establishment ($f_{dens}$) is modelled as in
@Sitch:2003wg:

$$
\label{eq-veg-est_dens}
f_{dens} = MAX(FPC_{max} - FPC, 0)
$$

Three types of mortality are considered as additive processes, growth-efficiency related mortality
($mort_{greff}$), density dependent mortality ($mort_{dens}$), and a PFT-specific background
mortality, representing currently unaccounted disturbance processes.

$$
\label{eq-mort-tot}
f_{mort} = MIN(mort_{greff} + mort_{dens} + mort_{bg,PFT}, 1)
$$

Growth-efficiency mortality, represents any kind of mortality associated with trees lacking the
ability to defend themselves against stress (e.g. pathogens) and is calculated as:

$$
\label{eq-veg-mort-greff}
\begin{align}
mort_{greff} &= \frac{k1_{mort\_greff}}{1 + k2_{mort\_greff} \times eff_{growth}}, where \\
&eff_{growth} = \frac{NPP - \sum{Turnover_i}}{LAI} 
\end{align}
$$

where, as in @Sitch:2003wg, $k1_{mort\_greff}$ and $k2_{mort\_greff}$ are parameters and growth
efficiency depends on net primary production minus tissue turnover (of all tissues $i$) per unit
leaf area, calculated as running means over $\tau_{mavg}^{dynamics}$.

Space constraints in tree populations (as for grasses $FPC$ is zero) are considered by constraining
the foliage projected cover to a prescribed maximum ($FPC_{max}$):

$$
\label{eq-veg-mort-selfthining}
mort_{dens} = MAX(FPC - FPC_{max},0)
$$

Litterfall from vegetation dynamics is then the product of the current pool size and $f_{mort}$,
scaled to the timestep of the model.

For trees, the appropriate number of individuals is also removed following mortality. This does not
affect the size of trees, as woody biomass and stand density are modified proportionally. In total,
the change in vegetation individual density following establishment and mortality is written as:

$$
\label{eq-veg-dens-ind}
\frac{dens_{ind}}{dt} = f_{mort} \times dens_{ind} + \frac{flux_{est,C}}{k_{seed}}
$$

where $flux_{est,C}$ is the carbon flux defined by [Eq. 3.34](#eq-veg:flux_est), and $k_{seed}$ is
the PFT-specific seed size.

## Herbivory

Biomass loss due to herbivory is represented for land cover classes (LCC) grassland and pasture. Representation of herbivory is based on the observation that biomass removal from herbivores in grasslands can be predicted by a power-law of grassland productivity (@McNaughton:1989na,@Cyr:1993na). As observed, the fraction of biomass removed increases with increasing productivity, which is implemented here by fitting the parameter $k^{LCC}_{herbivory}$ to their data and imposing a minimum annual productivity of $NPP^{LCC,min}_{herbivory}$. 

$$
\begin{align}
fract_{herbivory} = k^{LCC}_{herbivory} \times f^{lim}_{N} \times
 (NPP_{longterm}-NPP^{LCC,min}_{herbivory})^{\frac{4}{3}-1}
\end{align}
$$

where $fract_{herbivory}$ is set to zero is the grassland LAI is smaller than $LAI_{min}=0.1$ or $NPP_{longterm}$ is smaller that $NPP^{LCC,min}_{herbivory}$. $f^{lim}_{N}$ is a N limitation factor, which accounts for the reduced palatability of low nitrogen leaves, calculated as 

$$
f^{lim}_{N} = \frac{N_{leaf}}{C_{leaf}} \times \chi^{C:N}_{leaf,min},
$$

where $\chi^{C:N}_{leaf,min}$ is the PFT-specific minimum leaf C:N ratio. To represent energetic loss of carbon during herbivory, we assume that 90\% of the consumed biomass is respired immediately, whereas the remainder is added to the litter fall flux. Because of the tighter stoichiometry, the overall consequence is an increased net mineralisation rate.

# Soil biogeochemistry {#sec-soil-biogeochemistry}

The dynamics of the soil organic pools ($X$) are described in general as:

$$
\label{eq-total}
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial}{\partial t} X_{met} &= \sum(f_{vp \rightarrow met} F_{L_{vp}}) + f_{wl \rightarrow met} \eta_{wl \rightarrow met} \frac{X_{wl}}{\tau_{wl}} - \frac{X_{met}}{\tau_{met}}\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial t} X_{str} &= \sum(f_{vp \rightarrow str} F_{L_{vp}}) + f_{wl \rightarrow str} \eta_{wl \rightarrow str} \frac{X_{wl}}{\tau_{wl}}- \frac{X_{str}}{\tau_{str}}\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial t} X_{wl} &= \sum(f_{vp \rightarrow wl} F_{L_{vp}}) - \frac{X_{wl}}{\tau_{wl}}\\
\frac{\partial}{\partial t} X_{fast} &= \eta_{l \rightarrow {fast}} (\frac{X_{met}}{\tau_{met}} + \frac{X_{str}}{\tau_{str}}) + \eta_{{slow} \rightarrow {fast}} \frac{X_{slow}}{\tau_{slow}} - \frac{X_{fast}}{\tau_{fast}} + \Phi_{l \rightarrow {fast}} + \Phi_{{slow} \rightarrow {fast}} + \frac{\partial}{\partial z} (D_b \frac{\partial X_{fast}}{\partial z}) \\
\frac{\partial}{\partial t} X_{slow} &= \eta_{{fast} \rightarrow {slow}} \frac{X_{fast}}{\tau_{fast}} - \frac{X_{slow}}{\tau_{slow}}  + \Phi_{{fast} \rightarrow {slow}} + \frac{\partial}{\partial z} (D_b \frac{\partial X_{slow}}{\partial z})
\end{align}
$$

where $F_{L_{vp}}$ is the litterfall of the various plant tissue types, $f_{vp \rightarrow i}$ are
the coefficients determining the partitioning of this litterfall to the litter pools (see Section ),
$\tau_i$ are temperature and moisture adjusted, nitrogen-limited turnover times of the respective
pools (X; i = met, str, wl, fast, slow; see Section ), $\eta_{i \rightarrow j }$ are the mass
transfer from pool $i$ to $j$ (see Sect. @sec-sb-litter-partitioning), the $\Phi_x$ are the net mineralisation terms for N
and P, respectively, required to balance the carbon inflow to the fast and slow SOM pools and their
respective C:N:P stoichiometry (see Sect. @sec-sb-formation). The transfer of soil organic matter through
bioturbation is represented with a prescribed diffusion constant (see Sect. @sec-sb-bioturbation).

The dynamics of the inorganic nitrogen pools are described as:

$$
\label{eq-sb-simple-im-dynamics}
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial}{\partial t} NH_4 &= F_{dep,NH_4} - U_{plant,NH_4} - \sum(\Phi_{i,NH_4}) - U_{nit} - \frac{\partial v_{NH_4} NH_4}{\partial z} \\
    \frac{\partial}{\partial t} NO_3 &= F_{dep,NO_3} + F_{nit,NO3} - U_{plant,NO_3} - \sum(\Phi_{i,NO_3}) - U_{denit} - \frac{\partial v_{NO_3} NO_3}{\partial z} \\
    \frac{\partial}{\partial t} NO_y &= F_{nit,NO_y} + F_{denit,NO_y} - E_{NO_y} \\
    \frac{\partial}{\partial t} N_2O &= F_{nit,N_2O} + F_{denit,N_2O} - E_{N_2O} \\
\frac{\partial}{\partial t} N_2 &=  F_{nit,N_2} + F_{denit,N_2} - E_{N_2}
\end{align}
$$

where $U$ are the uptake rates of plants, or (de-)nitrifying bacteria, respectively (see Section and
, respectively); the $F_{dep}$ are the atmospheric deposition fluxes; the $F_{nit,i}$, and
$F_{denit,i}$ are the production of $\mathrm{NO_y}$, $\mathrm{N_2O}$ and $\mathrm{N_2}$ by
nitrification and denitrification, respectively; , and $\frac{\partial v_{x} X}{\partial z}$ the
vertical transport loss term given by the product of ion concentration and water mass flow between
soil layers (see Sect. ). Sorption of $\mathrm{NH_4}$ is not explicitly modelled, and is accounted
for by a reduced mobility in water ($f_{leach,{NH_4}}$).

The dynamics of the inorganic phosphorus pools are described as:

$$
\label{eq-sb-pi-dynamics}
\begin{align}
    \frac{\partial}{\partial t} PO_4 &= F_{dep,PO_4} + F_{weath,PO_4} + F_{biomin,PO_4} - U_{plant,PO_4} - F_{adsorp,PO_4} - \sum(\Phi_{i,PO_4}) -  \frac{\partial v_{PO_4} PO_4}{\partial z} \\
    \frac{\partial}{\partial t} P_{lab} &= F_{adsorp,PO_4} - F_{desorp,PO_4} + \frac{\partial}{\partial z} (D_b \frac{\partial P_{lab}}{\partial z}) \\
    \frac{\partial}{\partial t} P_{sorb} &= F_{desorp,PO_4} - F_{occlusion,PO_4} + \frac{\partial}{\partial z} (D_b \frac{\partial P_{sorb}}{\partial z}) \\
    \frac{\partial}{\partial t} P_{ocl} &= k_{ocl} P_{sorb} + \frac{\partial}{\partial z} (D_b \frac{\partial P_{ocl}}{\partial z}) \\
    \frac{\partial}{\partial t} P_{primary} &= - F_{weath,PO_4}
\end{align}
$$

where $P_{lab}$, $P_{sorb}$, $P_{ocl}$, and $P_{primary}$ are labile, absorbed, occluded, and
primary P, respectively; the $F_{dep,PO_4}$, $F_{weath,PO_4}$, $F_{biomin,PO_4}$, $F_{adsorp,PO_4}$,
and $F_{adsorp,PO_4}$ are the atmospheric deposition, weathering, fast adsorption, and phosphorus
fluxes, respectively (see Section ). All pools except the primary phosphorus pool are assumed to be
affected by bioturbation (see Sect. ).

## Partitioning of litterfall to litter pools {#sec-sb-litter-partitioning}

Non-woody litterfall is partitioned to the metabolic and structural litter according to the CENTURY
approach [@Parton:1993ud]. Litter from labile and reserve pools is assumed to enter the metabolic
pools, litter from sap- and heartwood enters the woody pool. The metabolic fraction of litterfall
from each vegetation pool ($_{vp}$, i.e. leaves, fine and coarse roots, fruits and seed-bed) is
determined as:

$$
\label{eq-sb-simple-litterpartitioning-c}
f_{vp \rightarrow met,C} = f_{met,max,C} - k_{met,C} \times LC_{vp} \frac{C_{vp}}{N_{vp}}
$$

where $f_{vp \rightarrow met,C}$ is constrained to positive solutions, $f_{met,max,C}$ is the
maximum fraction allocated to the metabolic pool, $k_{met,C}$ a factor relating the metabolic litter
fraction to the lignin to nitrogen ratio, $LC_{vp}$ the tissue-specific fraction of the lignin
content of that tissue type, and $\frac{C_{vp}}{N_{vp}}$ the C:N ratio of litterfall from that
tissue. The lignin content is assumed constant for all but the leaf tissues. For the latter, an
empirical dependency between lignin content and specific leaf-area ($sla$) is used [@White:2000vl].

$$
\label{eq-sb-simple-leaf-lc}
LC_{leaf} = LC_{leaf,max} + k_{leaf2sla} \times sla
$$

The remainder of litterfall is allocated to the structural pool. For N and P, the partitioning
assumes that the relative proportions of C:N and N:P are preserved in the partitioning according to:

$$
\label{eq-sb-simple-litterpartitioning-np}
f_{vp \rightarrow met,X} = \frac{1}{1+\frac{1-f_{vp \rightarrow met,C}}{k_{met,vp,X} \times f_{vp \rightarrow met,C}}}
$$

Woody decomposition is assumed to be a two-stage process. The first step implies physical
destabilisation and a first level of biochemical processing, which releases a constant fraction of
carbon (1 - $\eta_{C,wl \rightarrow met,str}$) to heterotrophic respiration. During this step, a
fraction of the nutrients (1 - $\eta_{N}|\eta_{P}$) is leached to the mineral phase to account for
inefficiencies of the microbiota in mineral processing decomposing wood. The remainder is assumed to
enter the metabolic and structural litter ([Eq. 4.12](#eq-sb:simple_litterpartitioning_c) and [Eq.
4.14](#eq-sb:simple_litterpartitioning_np)).

## SOM and litter turnover rates {#sec-sb-turnover}

The turnover times ($\tau^{base}_i$) of the litter and SOM pools respond to soil temperature
($T_{soil}$) and soil matrix potential ($\Psi_{soil}$) as follows:

$$
\label{eq-sb-simple-som-turnover}
\begin{align}
\tau^{*}_i &= \tau^{base}_i \times f(T_{soil}) \times g(\Psi_{soil}),\ where\\
f(T_{soil}) &= \frac{E_{d,decomp} \times e^{E_{a,decomp} \times T}}{E_{d,decomp} - E_{a,decomp} \times ( 1 - e^{E_{d,decomp} \times T})},\ with\\
T &= \frac{T_{soil} - T_{opt,decomp}}{T_{soil} \times T_{opt,decomp} \times R},\ and \\ 
g(\Psi_{soil}) &= 1 - \Psi_{soil} / \Psi_{dec,min}
\end{align}
$$

## SOM formation {#sec-sb-formation}

Matter entering the fast and slow SOM pool ([Eq. 4.1](#eq-sb:simple_om_dynamics)) is required to
fulfill the prescribed stoichiometry of the SOM pools ($\chi_{SOM}$). These are assumed constant
with the exception of the fast SOM C:N ratio, which varies with available $\mathrm{NH_4}$ following
CENTURY [@Parton:1993ud]:

$$
\label{eq-sb-SOMCNfast}
\chi_{SOM_{fast}^{C:N}} = MAX(\chi_{SOM_{fast,max}^{C:N}} - f_{\chi} \times NH_4,\chi_{SOM_{fast,min}^{C:N}})
$$

where $\chi_{SOM_{fast,min}^{C:N}}$, $\chi_{SOM_{fast,max}^{C:N}}$ and $f_{\chi}$ are parameters.

The difference in stoichiometry of the matter entering the pool and the required stoichiometry of
the pool leads to the estimate of the potential immobilisation flux:

$$
\label{eq-sb-simple-pot-n-immobilisation}
\Phi^{*}_{l \rightarrow {fast}, NH_4} = \frac{\eta_{C,litter \rightarrow fast}}{\chi_{SOM_{fast}^{C:N}}} (\frac{C_{met}}{\tau^{*}_{met}} + \frac{C_{str}}{\tau^{*}_{str}}) - \eta_N (\frac{N_{met}}{\tau^{*}_{met}} + \frac{N_{str}}{\tau^{*}_{str}})
$$

where $\tau^{*}_i$ are the temperature and moisture constrained turnover times ([Eq.
4.15](#eq-sb-simple-som-turnover)).

The actual immobilisation rate ($\Phi_{l \rightarrow {fast}, NH_4}$) is limited to the amount of
ammonium ($\mathrm{NH_4}$ available, subject to co-occurring potential N uptake from plants
($U^{*}_{NH_4,plant}$, [Eq. 4.23](#eq-sb-simple-potential-uptake)), and nitrifiers ($U^{*}_{nit}$;
[Eq. 4.26](#eq-sb-simple-dynamic-nitrification)). Note that, similar as for the plant uptake, the
uptake of ammonium is limited with a Michaelis-Menten kinetic to account for reduced accessibility
of N at very low values.

$$
\label{eq-sb-simple-act-n-immobilisation}
\Phi_{l \rightarrow {fast}, NH_4} = \frac{NH_4}{max(NH_4, \ U^{*}_{NH_4,plant} + U^{*}_{nit} + \Phi^{*}_{l \rightarrow {fast}, NH_4})} \times {\Phi^{*}_{l \rightarrow {fast}, NH_4}}
$$

In the case that $\Phi_{l \rightarrow {fast}, NH_4}$ is insufficient to ensure that the newly formed
fast SOM has a C:N ratio of $\chi_{SOM_{fast}^{C:N}}$, the turnover times of the metabolic and
structural litter pool is increased to match the N available for immobilisation [@Parton:1993ud]:

$$
\tau_{met|str} = \tau^{*}_{met|str} \frac{\frac{\eta_{l \rightarrow {fast},C}}{\chi_{SOM_{fast}^{C:N}}} (\frac{C_{met}}{\tau^{*}_{met}} + \frac{C_{str}}{\tau^{*}_{str}}) - \eta_N (\frac{N_{met}}{\tau^{*}_{met}} + \frac{N_{str}}{\tau^{*}_{str}})}{\Phi_{l \rightarrow {fast},NH_4}}
$$

Should the available $\mathrm{NH_4}$ be insufficient to maintain the uptake rates of plants ([Eq.
4.23](#eq-sb:simple_potential_uptake)) and nitrifiers ([Eq.
4.26](#eq-sb:simple_dynamic_nitrification)), these fluxes are downregulated in proportion.

The potential immobilisation flux of phosphorus ($\Phi^{*}_{P,l \rightarrow {fast}}$) is defined in
a similar manner as potential $NH_4$ immobilisation, but now considering the actual turnover time of
the litter pools:

$$
\label{eq-sb-simple-pot-p-immobilisation}
\begin{align}
\Phi^{*}_{P,l \rightarrow {fast}} &= \frac{\eta_{C,litter \rightarrow {fast}}}{\chi_{{SOM}_{fast}^{C:N}}\chi_{{SOM}_{fast}^{N:P}}} (\frac{C_{met}}{\tau_{met}} + \frac{C_{str}}{\tau_{str}}) -
\eta_P (\frac{P_{met}}{\tau_{met}} + \frac{P_{str}}{\tau_{str}})\\
\Phi_{P,l \rightarrow {fast}} &= \frac{PO_4}{max(PO_4, \ U^{*}_{PO_4,plant} + \Phi^{*}_{P,l \rightarrow {fast}})} \times {\Phi^{*}_{P,l \rightarrow {fast}}}
\end{align}
$$

Because the C:N:P stoichiometry and uptake use-efficiencies are organised such that decomposition of
these pools is always leading to net mineralisation of nutrients, the
$\Phi_{{slow} \rightarrow {fast}}$ values are negative and do not require special treatment to
affect the carbon-use efficiency or turnover rates (i.e. $\tau_{fast}=\tau_{fast}^{*}$, and
$\tau_{slow}=\tau_{slow}^{*}$). The processing of fast and slow SOM is assumed to also include
higher-order trophic levels of heterotrophic respiration [@Parton:1993ud], therefore only a fraction
of the respired material ($\eta_{C, {fast} \rightarrow {slow}}$ and
$\eta_{C, {slow} \rightarrow {fast}}$) is assumed to enter the subsequent pool:

$$
\label{eq-sb-mineralization}
\begin{align}
\Phi_{{fast} \rightarrow {slow},NH_4} &= \frac{\frac{\eta_{C, {fast} \rightarrow {slow}}}{\chi_{{SOM}_{slow}^{C:N}}} C_{fast} - N_{fast}}{\tau_{fast}} \\
\Phi_{{slow} \rightarrow {fast},NH_4} &= \frac{\frac{\eta_{C, {slow} \rightarrow {fast}}}{\chi_{{SOM}_{fast}^{C:N}}} C_{slow} - N_{slow}}{\tau_{slow}} \\
\Phi_{{fast} \rightarrow {slow},PO_4} &= \frac{\frac{\eta_{C, {fast} \rightarrow {slow}}}{\chi_{{SOM}_{slow}^{C:N}}\chi_{{SOM}_{slow}^{N:P}}} C_{fast} - P_{fast}}{\tau_{fast}} \\
\Phi_{{slow}\rightarrow {fast},PO_4} &= \frac{\frac{\eta_{C, slow \rightarrow fast}}{\chi_{{SOM}_{fast}^{C:N}}\chi_{{SOM}_{fast}^{N:P}}} C_{slow} - P_{slow}}{\tau_{slow}} - F_{biomin,PO_4}
\end{align}
$$

## Bioturbation {#sec-sb-bioturbation}

Bioturbation is treated as simple diffusive flux with a rate constant $D_b$, as in [@Ahrens:2015ie],
but declining with soil depth in proportion to the fraction of roots in the layer to account for
reduced biological activity with increasing soil depth:

$$
\label{eq-sb-bioturbation}
\begin{align}
D_b &= \frac{root_{frac}}{dz} \times \frac{k_{org}^{diff}}{\rho_{soil}^{cor}}, \ and\\
\rho_{soil}^{cor} &= MAX(\rho_{org}^{bulk}, \rho_{OM} + \rho_{soil} - \rho_{OM}\frac{\rho_{soil}}{\rho_{org}^{bulk}})
\end{align}
$$

where $root_{frac}$ and $dz$ are the root fraction and depth of the soil layer, $\rho_{soil}^{cor}$
is the soil bulk density corrected with soil organic matter, $\rho_{org}^{bulk}$ is the bulk density
of organic material, $\rho_{OM}$ is the organic matter density of the soil layer which depends on
the organic matter content in the soil layer, $\rho_{soil}$ is the bulk density of fine mineral
soil, and $k_{org}^{diff}$ is the diffusion coefficient for organic material due to bioturbation.

## Plant uptake rates {#sec-sb-simple-uptake}

The potential uptake rates of plants for X= $\mathrm{NH_4}$, $\mathrm{NO_3}$, and $\mathrm{PO_4}$
follow an extended Michaelis-Menten kinetics:

$$
\label{eq-sb-simple-potential-uptake}
\begin{align}
U^{*}_X &= v_{max,X}(T_{soil},\Psi) \times X \times (K_{m1,X}(T_{soil},\Theta)+ \frac{1}{K_{m2,X}(T_{soil},\Theta) + X}) \times f^X_{demand} \times C_{fine\_root},\ where\\
&v_{max,X}(T_{soil},\Psi) = v_{max,X} \frac{E_{d,uptake} \times e^{E_{a,uptake} \times T}}{E_{d,uptake} - E_{a,uptake} \times ( 1 - e^{E_{d,uptake} \times T})} \times \frac{\Psi_{fine\_root}}{\Psi_{leaf,min}},\ with\\
&T = \frac{T_{soil} - T_{opt,uptake}}{T_{soil} \times T_{opt,uptake} \times R},\ and \\ 
&K_{m1,X}(T_{soil},\Theta) = K_{m1,X} / (e^{-\frac{Ea,hsc}{R} \times (\frac{1}{T_{soil}} - \frac{1}{T^{\tau}_{ref}})} \times (\frac{\Theta}{\Theta_{fc}})^{k_{hsc}}),\ and\\
&K_{m2,X}(T_{soil},\Theta) = K_{m2,X} \times e^{-\frac{Ea,hsc}{R} \times (\frac{1}{T_{soil}} - \frac{1}{T^{\tau}_{ref}})} \times (\frac{\Theta}{\Theta_{fc}})^{k_{hsc}},\ and\\
&f^X_{demand} = 1 - e^{-(\frac{\chi^{X:Y}_{max}-\chi^{X:Y}_{labile}}{\chi^{X:Y}_{max} \times (1 - K_{demand}^{half,X})})^{k_{demand}}}  
\end{align}
$$

where $v_{max,X}$ is the PFT-specific temperature-sensitive maximum uptake rate per unit biomass,
adjusted by the current root zone moisture potential ($\Psi_{fine_root}$) to account for limited
transport of nutrients towards the roots in dry soils, $C_{fine\_root}$ is the biomass density of
fine roots ($\mathrm{mol \ C \ m^{-3}}$, see [Eq. 1.4](#eq-veg:root_distribution)), $T_{soil}$ is
the soil temperature and the $K_m$ parameters are nutrient sensitivities of the low and high
affinity transporters. These affinities are assumed to be temperature sensitive and are adjusted to
soil moisture to account for the difference between mass-based and soil solution concentrations
[@Ahrens:2015ie]. The potential uptake of nutrients can be down-regulated by plants given their
internal demand $f^X_{demand}$, where $X$ refers to either N or P and $X:Y$ refers to either N:C or
P:N ratios. $\chi^{X:Y}_{max}$ corresponds to the X:Y ratio of growing a unit of leaves and fine
roots at the current leaf-to-root ratio (see , $K_{demand}^{half, X}$ is a parameter denoting the
fraction of $\chi^{X:Y}_{max}$ at which uptake is reduced to 50% and $k_{demand}$ is shape
parameter.

## Asymbiotic biological nitrogen fixation {#sec-sb-asymb-bnf}

The asymbiotic biological nitrogen fixation (BNF) is represented as:

$$
\label{eq-sb-asymb-bnf}
F_{BNF}^{NH_4} = v_{max,BNF} \times f(T_{soil})
$$

where $v_{max,BNF}$ is a parameter representing the base rate of fixation and the temperature
response is calculated as above ([Eq. 4.15](#eq-sb-simple-som-turnover)). $BNF$ is suppressed if the
sum of $\mathrm{NH_4}$ and $\mathrm{NO_3}$ exceeds a critical threshold $N_{limit}^{BNF}$
[@Zaehle:2010a]. The distribution of $F_{BNF}^{NH_4}$ across soil layers follows the distribution of
fine roots, as indicator for C inputs into the soil. All N fixed through this mechanism is added to
the mineral $\mathrm{NH_4}$ soil pool.

## Nitrification and denitrification {#sec-sb-nitrification-denitrification}

Calculation of nitrification and denitrification follows [@XURI:2008jq; @Zaehle:2011gy], which
relies on the separation of the soil into aerobic and anaerobic volume fractions ($anvf$):

$$
\label{eq-sb-simple-anaerobic-vf}
\begin{align}
anvf &= e^{-(\lambda_{anvf} \times (1-afps))^{k_{anvf}}}, where\\
&afps = \frac{W_{fc}-W_{soil}}{W_{fc}} 
\end{align}
$$

where $\lambda_{anvf}$ and $k_{anvf}$ are parameters, $afps$ is the air filled pore space, and the
$W_x$ are the soil moisture contents as defined in Sect. .

The potential rate of nitrification ($U^{*}_{nit}$) in the aerobic fraction of the soil is modified
by temperature and soil moisture according to:

$$
\label{eq-sb-simple-dynamic-nitrification}
\begin{align}
U^{*}_{nit} &= v_{max,nit} \times f(T_{soil}) \times g(\Theta) \times NH_4, where\\
&f(T_{soil}) = E_{d,nit} \frac{e^{\frac{E_{a,nit}\times kt}{R_{gas}}}}{E_{d,nit}-E_{a,nit}\times (1 - e^{\frac{E_{d,nit} \times kt}{R_{gas}}})} \\
&kt = \frac{T_{soil}-T_{opt,nit}}{T_{soil} \times T_{opt,nit}}\\
&g(\Theta) = 1-afps
\end{align}
$$

The actual rate of nitrification ($U_{nit}$), given the potential rate and competing demands from
plant and microbial uptake (Sect. , is partitioned into its products ($\mathrm{NO_3}$,
$\mathrm{NO_y}$, and $\mathrm{N_2O}$) according to

$$
\label{eq-sb-simple-dynamic-nitrification-prod}
\begin{align}
F_{nit,NO_3} &= (1 - f_{nit}^{NO_y} - f_{nit}^{N_2O}) \times U_{nit}\\
F_{nit,NO_y} &= f_{nit}^{NO_y}  \times U_{nit}\\
F_{nit,N_2O} &= f_{nit}^{N_2O}  \times U_{nit}
\end{align}
$$

where the $F_{nit,X}$ are the nitrification fluxes for $\mathrm{NO_3}$, $\mathrm{NO_y}$, and
$\mathrm{N_2O}$, respectively ([Eq. 4.3](#eq-sb-simple-im-dynamics-b), [Eq.
4.4](#eq-sb-simple-im-dynamics-c) and [Eq. 4.5](#eq-sb-simple-im-dynamics-d)).

The potential rate of denitrification ($U^{*}_{denit}$) in the anaerobic fraction of the soil is
modified by temperature:

$$
\label{eq-sb-simple-dynamic-denitrification}
\begin{align}
U^{*}_{denit} &= anvf \times v_{max,denit}(T_{soil}) \times \frac{C_{fast}}{K_{m,denit}^{fast} + C_{fast}} \frac{NO_3}{K_{m,denit}^{NO_3} + NO_3}, where\\
&v_{max,denit}(T_{soil}) = v_{max,denit} \times e^{-\frac{E_{a,denit}}{R} \times (\frac{1}{T_{soil}} - \frac{1}{T^{\tau}_{ref}})}
\end{align}
$$

The actual rate of denitrification ($U_{denit}$), given the potential rate and competing demands
from plant uptake (Sect. , is partitioned into its products ($\mathrm{NO_y}$, $\mathrm{N_2O}$, and
$\mathrm{N_2}$) according to

$$
\label{eq-sb-simple-dynamic-denitrification-prod}
\begin{align}
F_{denit,NO_y} &= f_{denit}^{NO_y}  \times U_{denit}\\
F_{denit,N_2O} &= f_{denit}^{N_2O}  \times U_{denit}\\
F_{denit,N_2} &= (1 - f_{denit}^{NO_y} - f_{denit}^{NO_y}) \times U_{denit}
\end{align}
$$

where the $F_{denit,X}$ are the denitrification fluxes for $\mathrm{NO_y}$, $\mathrm{N_2O}$, and
$\mathrm{N_2}$, respectively ([Eq. 4.3](#eq-sb:simple_im_dynamics_b), [Eq.
4.4](#eq-sb:simple_im_dynamics_c) and [Eq. 4.5](#eq-sb:simple_im_dynamics_d)). The model currently
ignores the effect of ammonia volatilisation, which is of low relevance for natural, unfertilised
ecosystems.

## Phosphorus weathering and biomineralisation {#sec-sb-p_flux}

Weathering is modelled following [@Wang:2010ba] as:

$$
\label{eq-sb-weathering}
\begin{align}
F_{weath,PO_4} &=f(T_{soil}) \times g(\Theta) \times f(C_{fine\_root}) \times k_{weath} \times \rho_{soil}^{cor},\ where\\
&f(T_{soil}) = e^{-\frac{Ea,hsc}{R} \times (\frac{1}{T_{soil}} - \frac{1}{T^{\tau}_{ref}})},\\
&g(\Theta) =(\frac{\Theta}{\Theta_{fc}})^3, and \\
&f(C_{fine\_root}) =\frac{C_{fine\_root}}{K_{m,weath}^{root}+C_{fine\_root}}
\end{align}
$$

where $k_{weath}$ is the rate constant for weathering, and $\rho_{soil}^{cor}$ is the soil bulk
density corrected by SOM content. The weathering rate decreases with soil depth as the fine root C
decreases and is modified by soil temperature and moisture.

The potential biomineralisation rate of $\mathrm{PO_4}$ is determined as an additional turnover of
the P contained in the slow SOM pool, modified by temperature and moisture modifiers, and affected
by the concentration of $PO_4$ and the root biomass:

$$
\label{eq-sb-p-biomin}
\begin{align}
F^{*}_{biomin,PO_4} &= \frac{C_{slow}}{\chi_{{SOM}_{slow}^{C:N}} \times \chi_{{SOM}_{slow}^{N:P}} \times \tau_{biomin}} \times f(C_{fine\_root})  \times f(PO_4) \times  f(T_{soil}) \times  g(\Theta),\ where\\
&f(C_{fine\_root}) = \frac{C_{fine\_root}}{K_{m,biomin}^{root} + C_{fine\_root}},\ and\\
&f(PO_4) = \frac{K_{m,biomin}^{PO_4}}{K_{m,biomin}^{PO_4}+PO_4}
\end{align}
$$

where $K_{m,biomin}^{root}$ and $K_{m,biomin}^{PO_4}$ are constants constraining the
biomineralisation rate under low root biomass and high $PO_4$ concentration, respectively; the
temperature and moisture responses are calculated as those in [Eq.
4.15](#eq-sb:simple_som_turnover). The biomineralisation rate is further constrained so that it does
not alter the stoichiometry of the fast pool.

$$
F_{biomin,PO_4} = MIN(F^{*}_{biomin,PO_4}, \frac{\frac{\eta_{C, {slow} \rightarrow {fast}}}{\chi_{{SOM}_{slow}^{C:N}}\chi_{{SOM}_{slow}^{N:P}}} C_{slow} - P_{slow}}{\tau_{slow}})
$$

## Phosphorus adsorption and (ab)sorption {#sec-phosphorus-adsorption-and-absorption}

$\mathrm{PO_4}$ desorption is modelled as:

$$
\label{eq-sb-pi-desorp}
\begin{align}
F_{desorp,PO_4} &=f(T_{soil},E_{a,abs}) \times  k_{abs}   \times P_{lab} - f(T_{soil},E_{a,des})   \times k_{des}   \times P_{sorb},\ where\\
&f(T_{soil,E_a}) = e^{-\frac{E_{a}}{R} \times (\frac{1}{T_{soil}} - \frac{1}{T^{\tau}_{ref}})}
\end{align}
$$

where $k_{abs}$ and $k_{des}$ are the rate constants of (ab)sorption and desorption, and $E_{a,abs}$
and $E_{a,des}$ the respective activation energies.

The adsorption ($F_{adsorp,PO_4}$) flux from soil solution to the soil adsorption sites is
calculated assuming constant Langmuir equilibrium [@Barrow:1978] between soluble and adsorbed P:

$$
\label{eq-sb-langmuir-a}
\begin{align}
PO_4 &= \frac{S_{max} \times PO_4}{K_S + PO_4}, \\
    &\textrm{thus} \nonumber \\
&\frac{\partial P_{lab}}{\partial t} = \frac{S_{max}\times PO_4}{(K_S + PO_4)^2} \frac{\partial PO_4}{\partial t}, \\
\end{align}
$$

[and by rearranging]{.roman}

$$
\label{eq-sb-langmuir-b}
\begin{align}
    \frac{\partial P_{lab}}{\partial t} &= k_{p}\frac{\partial {(P_{lab}+PO_4)}}{\partial t} &\\
    \frac{\partial PO_4}{\partial t} &= (1-k_{p})\frac{\partial {(P_{lab}+PO_4)}}{\partial t},\ where &\\
    &k_p = \frac{S_{max}\times PO_4}{(K_S + PO_4)^2+S_{max}PO_4}, &
\end{align}
$$

where $S_{max}$ and $K_S$ are the maximum sorption capacity, and the half-saturation concentration
coefficient of the soil, and are modified by soil moisture and SOM content as follows:

$$
\label{eq-sb-Psorbpar}
\begin{align}
S_{max} &= \Theta_{soil} \times (S^{max}_{om} V^{frac}_{om} \rho_{org}^{bulk} + S^{max}_{mineral} V^{frac}_{mineral} \rho_{soil}), \ and\\
K_S &=  K^{sorb}_{m,om} V^{frac}_{om} \rho_{org}^{bulk} + K^{sorb}_{m,mineral} V^{frac}_{mineral} \rho_{soil}
\end{align}
$$

where $V^{frac}_{om}$ and $V^{frac}_{mineral}$ are volumetric fractiosn of organic matter and fine
soil minerals, respectively. $S^{max}_{om}$ and $S^{max}_{mineral}$ are the maximum $\mathrm{PO_4}$
sorption capacity of pure organic matter and pure fine soil, respectively. $K^{sorb}_{m,om}$ and
$K^{sorb}_{m,mineral}$ are the half-saturation concentration coefficient of pure organic matter and
pure fine soil, respectively.

Based on [Eq. 4.6](#eq-sb-simple-im-dynamics-e) and [Eq. 4.7](#eq-sb-pi-dynamics-a), the equilibrium
in [Eq. 4.35](#eq-sb-langmuir-b) could be solved.

$$
\begin{split}
\frac{\partial {(P_{lab}+PO_4)}}{\partial t} &= F_{dep,PO_4} + F_{weath,PO_4} + F_{biomin,PO_4} - U_{plant,PO_4} - U_{myc,PO_4} - F_{desorp,PO_4}\\
&- \sum(\Phi_{i,PO_4}) -  \frac{\partial v_{PO_4} PO_4}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial}{\partial z} (D_b \frac{\partial P_{lab}}{\partial z})\\
\end{split}
$$

## Soil in- and outfluxes {#sec-sb-simple-netbalance}

Currently, gas diffusion is not modelled explicitly. Instead, $\mathrm{CO_2}$ is assumed to be
directly released to the atmosphere. The carbon efflux per soil layer is described as:

$$
F^{\uparrow}_{CO_2} = ( (1-\eta_{C,litter \rightarrow fast}) (\frac{C_{met}}{\tau_{met}} + \frac{C_{str}}{\tau_{str}}) + (1 - \eta_{C,wl \rightarrow met|str}) \frac{C_{wl}}{\tau_{wl}} + (1 - \eta_{C,fast \rightarrow slow}) \frac{C_{fast}}{\tau_{fast}} + (1 - \eta_{C,slow \rightarrow fast}) \frac{C_{slow}}{\tau_{slow}} ) \Delta t,
$$

and similar for $\mathrm{^{13}C}$ and $\mathrm{^{14}C}$ fluxes. Slightly differently from that, the
emission of gaseous N species is assumed to follow [@XURI:2008jq], which considers the effect of
temperature and moisture on gas loss. However, transfer between soil layers is equally not treated
explicitly.

$$
\label{eq-sb-simple-ngasloss}
\begin{align}
F^{\uparrow}_{X} &= f(T_{soil}) \times afps \times X, where \\
f(T_{soil}) &= e^{-\frac{E_{a,diff}}{R} \times (\frac{1}{T_{soil}} - \frac{1}{T^{\tau}_{ref}})}
\end{align}
$$

and $afps$ is the air-filled pore fraction of the soil (see [Eq. 4.25](#eq-sb-simple-anaerobic-vf).)

## Isotopic composition and fractionation {#sec-isotopic-composition-and-fractionation}

The carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) flows and pool tracked in the model are comprising all major
isotopes (i.e. C = $\mathrm{^{12}C}$ + $\mathrm{^{13}C}$ + $\mathrm{^{14}C}$, and N =
$\mathrm{^{14}N}$ + $\mathrm{^{15}N}$). The model explicitly tracks the mass flow of
$\mathrm{^{13}C}$, $\mathrm{^{14}C}$ and $\mathrm{^{15}N}$ as separate entities for all
biogeochemical pools and fluxes. The molar mixing ratio ($R_X$) of the isotope (e.g.
$\mathrm{^{13}C)}$ to the main element (e.g. $\mathrm{^{12}C}$) of each biogeochemical pool can be
calculated as

$$
